statements.statement: It was usually clear which element of the project a scope change decision was about.
Scope change discussions often mixed technical, financial and planning issues, making it unclear what the decision was really about.
It was clear who had the authority to make final decisions on proposed scope changes.
Decisions about scope changes were often made by whoever happened to be most involved, rather than by the formally responsible party.
Agreements on who decides about what were consistently followed.
Scope change decisions were systematically documented, including the reasons and approvals.
Scope change decisions were prepared collaboratively, integrating the knowledge of each of the parties involved evenly.
Contractors were sometimes only pseudo-involved in scope change decisions, having limited actual influence.
The collaborative scope change process was documented and contextualized.
The project team generally reached consensus about what fell inside or outside the agreed scope.
Scope changes followed a structured sequence—initiation, evaluation, assessment, decision, and implementation.
Scope changes that evolved organically, without strict go/no-go decisions, were often more efficient and productive.
It was often unclear who raised a change, when, and why.
Change proposals were reviewed early to avoid uncontrolled development and duplicate assessment work.
Assessments of scope changes resulted in clear, updated documents such as revised risk registers or cost estimates.
Approval and escalation outcomes regarding scope changes were clearly recorded before implementation.
Every approved scope change was systematically implemented into the relevant bouwteam documents.
At all times, the project team knew which version of the contract documents was most recent.
The short bouwteam period made it difficult to balance formal documentation with informal discussions about scope changes.
During price formation, cost pressures often influenced how scope changes were framed or justified.
Ambiguity in earlier bouwteam decisions creates accountability issues during execution.
Combining responsibility for design and construction within one party reduces coordination and interface risks.
Combining responsibility for design and construction within one party increases that party’s exposure to uncertainty and risk.
In the realization phase, formal lines of authority leave limited space to maintain the open consultation that characterized the bouwteam.
When it is unclear who initiated a change during the bouwteam—or when and why—it becomes difficult to determine responsibilities later on.
Without formal approval of bouwteam decisions, it becomes difficult to hold parties accountable once the realization phase begins.
Implementation of bouwteam scope changes often starts before formal approval, making them hard to trace after transition.
At the transition from bouwteam to realization, client and contractor interests diverge: the client seeks certainty, while the contractor resists liability for incomplete bouwteam results.
Not all bouwteam results are formally included in the realization contract; some are deliberately left out to keep flexibility or limit risk.
Price and liability negotiations at the transition from bouwteam to realization frequently reopen earlier bouwteam agreements.
A tool that links requirements and scope would help prevent scope drift in bouwteam projects.
A change register that documents every change and its implications for the contract documents would improve traceability across phases.
A shared knowledge repository would strengthen inter-organizational learning and accountability in bouwteam projects.
A mechanism that translates collaborative bouwteam decisions into verifiable records that remain valid once realization begins would reduce disputes.
Digital traceability systems improve accountability but can make collaboration overly formal.
Setting clear moments to freeze the design would help create structure for the transition to realization.
Effective scope change tools depend more on behavioral discipline and ownership than on new software.
Overly formal procedures for transferring bouwteam agreements to realization can damage trust and openness.
Central oversight of documentation by the client improves traceability but weakens joint ownership of decisions.
